business_question: Can we tell a rider, at the moment they request a yellow cab, how long the trip will take and what it will cost -- accurately enough that they trust the number and plan around it?
success_criteria: Mean absolute duration error under 5 minutes on unseen future days.
Beat the dispatcher's distance-over-speed heuristic by a wide margin.
Publish an 80% interval whose empirical coverage is within 5 points of 80%.
No feature may use information unavailable at the moment of booking.

phases.title: 1. Business Understanding
phases.purpose: Translate a business question into a measurable data-mining goal and fix the success criteria before seeing any results.
phases.summary: A duration estimate is only useful if it is honest about uncertainty. A rider told '22 minutes' who arrives in 40 is worse off than one told '20-35 minutes'. We therefore committed up front to shipping an interval, not just a point estimate, and to scoring the interval's coverage as a first-class success criterion.
activities: Framed the task as dual regression: duration in minutes and fare in dollars.
Chose MAE over RMSE because riders experience absolute lateness.
Defined the booking-time information boundary: anything the meter produces during or after the trip is off limits as a feature.
Set three heuristic baselines that any model must beat to justify itself.

findings.statement: Tip, tolls and total fare are recorded post-trip
findings.implication: Excluded from the feature set; using them would leak the outcome into the prediction.

decisions.rationale: Lateness is felt linearly, and MAE is robust to the genuine multi-hour outliers the TLC publishes.
decisions.rejection_reason: Squared error lets a handful of corrupt 4-hour records dominate model selection.

decisions.decision: Ship an 80% prediction interval alongside the point estimate.
decisions.rationale: Uncertainty is the actionable part for trip planning.
decisions.rejection_reason: Implies a precision the model does not have.

criteria: Success criteria fixed before any modelling

phases.title: 2. Data Understanding
phases.purpose: Acquire the data, describe it honestly, and surface quality problems early enough that they can change the plan.
phases.summary: 150,000 trips sampled from the 2.96M the TLC published for January 2024, joined to the official 265-zone dictionary. The data is real, and so are its defects: the quality scorecard grades it A at 100.0%.
activities: Profiled all numeric and categorical fields with Tukey fences.
Built 7x24 demand and mean-duration heatmaps.
Joined LocationIDs to boroughs and zone names.
Cross-tabulated mean duration for all 36 borough pairs.

findings.statement: A visible minority of trips are physically impossible
findings.evidence: 6,312 rows (4.21%) violate at least one plausibility rule
findings.implication: Removed by stated rule, each exclusion counted and published.

findings.statement: Average speed collapses during the weekday peak
findings.implication: Motivated explicit rush-hour and cyclical-time features.

findings.statement: Trip distance is strongly but non-linearly related to duration
findings.evidence: Spearman exceeds Pearson across the correlation matrix
findings.implication: Signals that tree ensembles should beat linear models.

decisions.decision: Join the TLC zone lookup and model borough, not LocationID.
decisions.rationale: 265 arbitrary integers invite memorisation; 6 boroughs carry real geographic meaning.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Raw LocationID as a numeric feature
decisions.rejection_reason: Implies an ordering between zones that does not exist.

criteria: Defects documented rather than silently repaired

phases.title: 3. Data Preparation
phases.purpose: Construct the modelling dataset: selection, cleaning, feature engineering and the train/test protocol that makes evaluation trustworthy.
phases.summary: 143,688 trips survive the eight plausibility rules. Fifteen booking-time features are constructed; every fitted transformation lives inside the model pipeline.
activities: Applied 8 physical-plausibility filters, counting each exclusion.
Encoded hour and weekday cyclically so 23:00 neighbours 00:00.
Frequency-encoded the 265 zone IDs inside the pipeline.
One-hot encoded boroughs, rate codes and trip type with a rare-level floor.
Split chronologically at 2024-01-26 01:45:58.

findings.statement: No filter references the target distribution
findings.implication: Hard-but-real cases stay in the test set.

findings.evidence: 3 fitted transformers, all inside the Pipeline
findings.implication: Cross-validated scores are not optimistically biased.

decisions.rationale: Deployment predicts future trips from past ones; the evaluation must mirror that.
decisions.rejection_reason: Lets the model interpolate within a rush hour it has already seen, inflating the score.

decisions.decision: Frequency-encode zone IDs instead of one-hot.
decisions.rationale: Captures 'busy origin' in one column instead of 530.
decisions.rejection_reason: Target encoding needs careful nested CV to avoid leaking the label; the gain did not justify the risk.

criteria: All fitted transforms inside the Pipeline

phases.title: 4. Modeling
phases.purpose: Select techniques, search their hyperparameters, and record what was tried -- including what failed.
phases.summary: 79 hill-climbing trials across 6 model families, scored by expanding-window cross-validated MAE. 'XGBoost' won and was deployed.
activities: Seeded each family with a sane baseline configuration.
Ran coordinate-ascent hill climbing over discrete hyperparameter grids.
Refitted each family's winner on the full training half.
Fitted paired 10th/90th-percentile quantile models for intervals.
Trained a second model on fare using the identical feature set.

findings.statement: Search improved the champion by 0.007 minutes MAE over its seed
findings.implication: Modest gains: the feature set, not the hyperparameters, carries the performance.

findings.statement: Independently-fitted quantiles crossed on a minority of rows
findings.implication: A known artefact of separate quantile fits; repaired monotonically and reported, not hidden.

decisions.decision: Hill climbing rather than random or grid search.
decisions.rationale: Produces a readable improvement trajectory and reaches a good configuration in ~14 fits per family.
decisions.rejection_reason: Hundreds of fits for a fraction of a minute of MAE.

decisions.decision: Tune on cross-validated MAE, never on the hold-out.
decisions.rationale: The hold-out has to stay unseen to mean anything.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Early stopping against the test set
decisions.rejection_reason: Standard practice in tutorials and a direct leak.

criteria: Search ran only on training folds

phases.title: 5. Evaluation
phases.purpose: Assess results against the business criteria from phase 1, not just the loss function, and review the whole process for defects.
phases.summary: On the untouched final week the champion achieves 2.93 minutes MAE (R^2 0.836), against 6.29 for the best heuristic -- a 53% reduction in error. The 80% interval covers 77.3% of outcomes.
activities: Scored the held-out final week once.
Compared against three heuristic baselines.
Decomposed error by trip type, borough, rush hour and hour of day.
Tested interval coverage against its nominal 80%.
Cross-checked permutation against impurity importance.

findings.statement: Champion beats the best heuristic baseline

findings.implication: Riders can act on the band as stated.

findings.statement: Error is concentrated in airport trips
findings.implication: Airport runs have the widest genuine variance; the interval widens there rather than the point estimate being wrong.

decisions.decision: Report per-segment error, not just the aggregate.
decisions.rationale: An average hides which riders are served badly.
decisions.rejection_reason: Would conceal systematically worse airport estimates.

gate.notes: MAE 2.93 min against a 5.00 min target.

phases.title: 6. Deployment
phases.purpose: Ship the model behind an interface, with monitoring, documented limits, and a plan for the day the data drifts.
phases.summary: Served by FastAPI behind /api/projects/taxi/predict. The pipeline is pickled whole -- preprocessing travels with the model, so training and serving cannot drift apart.
activities: Pickled the fitted Pipeline including all preprocessing.
Exposed point estimate, 80% band, fare estimate and a SHAP waterfall.
Stamped artifacts with git commit, timestamp and platform.
Published the model card with documented limitations.

findings.statement: Training and serving share one code path
findings.evidence: the same Pipeline object is fitted and pickled
findings.implication: Removes the most common source of training/serving skew.

findings.statement: Model is fixed to January 2024 conditions
findings.implication: Congestion pricing and seasonality will drift; the card sets a quarterly retraining trigger.

decisions.decision: Pin artifacts to disk rather than recomputing per request.
decisions.rationale: The dashboard is a record of a specific, auditable run.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Recompute SHAP and metrics on every request
decisions.rejection_reason: Slow, and it would let the reported numbers drift silently between restarts.

iteration_notes: Phase 5 sent us back to phase 3: the first evaluation showed airport trips with double the error of city trips, which is why an explicit trip_type feature exists at all.
The interval was added after phase 1's review concluded that a bare point estimate would overstate what the data supports.
methodology: CRISP-DM (Cross-Industry Standard Process for Data Mining), Chapman et al. 2000. Phases are iterative; the notes below record where this project looped back rather than proceeding linearly.
